chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hisham ibn al-Hakam, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) regarding
two gutters that were flowing, one of them with urine and the other with rainwater, so they mixed together and struck the garment of a man — that would not harm him.

key_terms.اخْتَلَطَ: To mix together, intermingle — the key legal act triggering the ruling
key_terms.بَوْل: Urine (najis — a major source of ritual impurity in Islamic law)
key_terms.مَاءُ الْمَطَرِ: Rainwater — in Shia jurisprudence, running water including rainwater has purifying properties
key_terms.مِيزَاب: Drainage gutter/spout, typically referring to roof-level conduits channeling water

ai.seo_question: If urine mixes with rainwater in a drain and hits someone's clothes, is the clothing ritually impure?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) issues a legal ruling that when urine flowing from a drain mixes with rainwater and the mixture contacts a person's clothing, the garment remains ritually pure and the person is not harmed. This ruling reflects the Shia jurisprudential principle that rainwater (and its mixture) in sufficient flow can purify or neutralize najasah (ritual impurity). The original audience, students of fiqh in the early Abbasid period, would have understood this as a practical ruling for a common urban situation involving roof gutters in cities.
